extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers interested in American political institutions and their future
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic review of the forces and criteria that will shape the future of American political institutions (Federal system, branches of government, parties, and public life) from a late-19th/early-20th-century perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal system equilibrium / cohesion of the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: That equilibrium [of the Federal system] has been little disturbed... At this moment, however, nothing seems less likely than another secession. The States' Rights spirit has declined. The material interests of every part of the country are bound up with those of every other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Eastern capital invested in Western mines and Southern manufactures; Western produce flows through Eastern ports; travel and student migration knit regions together. Use economic interdependence, transport/communication linkages, and social ties as measures of Federal cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centripetal (unifying) vs centrifugal (disjunctive) forces
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to ignore the growing strength of the centripetal and unifying forces... Wherever in the modern world there has been a centrifugal movement the movement has sprung from a sentiment of nationality or from substantial grievance; when such forces are absent, aggregation and centralization prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors strengthening centripetal forces: easier/cheaper communications, commerce, telegraph, filling of vacant spaces. Assess presence/absence of national feeling (race, language, literature, political habits) and material interests to judge tendency toward centralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declining relative importance of States
rubrics_metrics.description: State autonomy, as well as local government within each State, is prized by every class... It may therefore be concluded that while there is no present likelihood of change from a Federal to a consolidated republic... the importance of the States will decline as the majesty and authority of the National government increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate social/moral role of States versus legal powers; factor in ambitions of office-seekers, popular attachment to localism, and federal expansion through legislation where state laws prove inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of federal legislation when State laws are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an increasing tendency to invoke congressional legislation to deal with matters, such as railroads, which cannot be adequately handled by State laws, or to remove divergencies, such as those in the law of marriage and divorce, which give rise to practical inconveniences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure frequency and scope of federal intervention on interstate economic and social issues (railroads, commerce, family law) as an indicator of centralizing tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance among national branches (stability and oscillation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The equilibrium [among national organs] stands now as stable as at any former epoch. Yet it has twice experienced violent oscillations... That no permanent disturbance of the balance followed shows how well the balance had been adjusted at starting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historical oscillations (e.g., Jackson, Lincoln, Tyler, Andrew Johnson) and current indicators (legislative usurpation, executive vigor, judicial rulings) to evaluate whether any branch is gaining permanent ascendancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congress's capacity, weaknesses, and public-opinion leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has been the branch... with the largest facilities for usurping the powers of the other branches... But although Congress has succeeded in occupying nearly all of the area which the Constitution left vacant... it has not become... the dominant power in the State. In a country ruled by public opinion, it could hold this position only in virtue of its capacity for leading opinion—courage, promptitude, and wisdom. Since it grows in no one of these qualities, it wins no greater ascendency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Congress by its ability to lead public opinion, internal organization (two Houses), quality and experience of members, susceptibility to self-interest, and effectiveness in constructive legislation; watch signs of declining esteem or inability to serve as principal law-maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential strength and the concentration of power
rubrics_metrics.description: The weakness of Congress is the strength of the President... The tendency everywhere in America to concentrate power and responsibility in one man is unmistakable. He may have a great part to play as the leader of the majority and the exponent of its will... possibilities of greatness... depend... on the wholly unpredictable element of personal capacity in the men who may fill the office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the presidency by (a) scope to represent and influence public opinion, (b) degree of power-concentration in practice, (c) the personal capacity/character of incumbents, and (d) popular tolerance of presidential leadership exercised through constitutional organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary's scope and changing role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Judiciary... seemed in 1880 to have less discretionary power than they had exerted fifty years earlier, for by their own decisions they had narrowed the scope of their discretion. But soon after new groups of questions arose, raising new issues for judicial determination... the rulings of the Supreme Court ever involved larger interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure judicial influence by the openness of legal questions, scope of discretionary interpretation, and the prominence/impact of Supreme Court decisions on national affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace of development vs institutional soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: As a town built in a hurry is seldom well built, so a society will be the sounder in health for not having grown too swiftly... the passion for speculation, the feverish eagerness for quick and showy results, may so soak into the texture of the popular mind as to colour it for centuries to come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether rapid material development sacrifices durable institutional quality—consider prevalence of lawlessness, lynch law, saloons/gambling-houses, and persistence of 'bad habits of professional politics' as negative indicators of too-rapid growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party-machine resilience and need for external reform
rubrics_metrics.description: The Machine will not be reformed from within: it must be assailed from without.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for weakening party machines: honest administration and extension of Civil Service Reform; adoption of secret ballot laws; enactment and operation of Primary Laws to take nominations out of machine control; presence of independent citizen movements, press and pulpit support, and educated public demanding purity in politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific reforms that attack the Spoils System / Machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Three heavy blows have been struck at it. The first was the Civil Service Reform Act of 1883... The second has been the passing of secret ballot laws... The third has been that uprising of independent citizens which has induced the enactment of the so-called Primary Laws...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use progress on these three concrete measures—merit-based civil service, secret ballots, and primaries—as direct metrics of success against machine politics; assess honest administration and diffusion to State and local levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher moral and intellectual standards in public life
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of purity among public men, especially in the Federal government, is higher. The number of able men who occupy themselves with scientific economics and politics is larger, their books and articles are more widely read. The press more frequently helps in the work of reform: the pulpit deals more largely with questions of practical philanthropy and public morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate public life improvement via indicators such as less blind party obedience, increased independent voting, prevalence of able/public-spirited candidates, press and pulpit engagement, and growth of scientific political discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immigration and national feeling (assimilation and lack of political danger)
rubrics_metrics.description: The immense influx of immigrants of various races speaking diverse languages has not greatly affected the sense of race unity, for the immigrant's child is eager to become... an American. Moreover, the immigrants are so dispersed over the country that no single section of them is in any State nearly equal to the native population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether immigration produces political danger by looking for concentrated immigrant enclaves exercising sectional political power; otherwise use assimilation trends and dispersion as signs that immigration does not threaten national cohesion.
